notes:
IS ORDER OBSERVABLE? Yes, but only implicitly. None of get_folder_tree / list_root_folders / list_folder_contents declares or returns a position/order/sequence field — order is inferable ONLY from array sequence (`contents`/`structure` in get_folder_tree, `folders`/`self.contents` in list_folder_contents), and that sequence does change and persist after a reorder call, confirmed across 5 separate before/after reads. So this capability's effect is verifiable, just not through any documented field — a caller has no supported way to assert on order besides diffing array positions.

HEADLINE FINDING — prev/next semantics are SWAPPED relative to the documented contract. The spec says prev='land after this id', next='land before this id'. Observed, across three independent trials: whenever `next` is supplied (attempts 1 and 2, whether or not `prev` was also given), the moved folder lands immediately AFTER next's pre-move position — the opposite of 'before'. When `next` is omitted and only `prev` is given (attempt 5), the moved folder lands immediately BEFORE prev's pre-move position — the opposite of 'after'. In other words the two parameters behave exactly as if their names were exchanged: `prev` actually means 'land before this id' and `next` actually means 'land after this id'. When both are supplied, `next`'s 'land after' behaviour wins and `prev` has no independent effect on final position (attempt 2). This is a silent, high-impact defect: every 200 response looks identical ({success:true, message:'Folders reordered successfully'}) whether or not the folder landed where the documented contract promised, so a caller following the docs literally will consistently place folders one slot off from where they intended, with no error signal at all.

PARTIAL-LIST BEHAVIOUR: unlike edit_test_run.test_case_ids' destructive-replace precedent, `current` here is genuinely additive/minimal. Across all 5 reorder calls (each moving only 1 of the 7 siblings), the 6 folders NOT named in `current` kept both their parent (764138 throughout — sub_folders_count stayed 7 every time, get_folder_tree confirmed every id's parent_id unchanged) and their relative order among themselves. Nothing was appended-to-end, dropped, or reparented for being omitted from `current`. This capability does NOT reproduce the edit_test_run bug — omitted siblings are left alone.

CROSS-PARENT ID: sending an id from a different parent (765817, actually a child of 765811) anchored against 764138's siblings returned 200 {success:true} but was a complete no-op on 765817 — no reparenting, but also no error or partial-failure indication. This is the 'silent 200 half-success' bad-id behaviour category, applied here to a wrong-parent id rather than a nonexistent one. No data-integrity breach (765817 stayed exactly where it was), but the response cannot be trusted to mean 'everything in current was moved'.

BAD ID (nonexistent folder, 999999999): clean 400, but body shape is `{success:false, message:'The API request is invalid or improperly formed'}` — flat, no `error:{code,message,details}` object at all, unlike either declared error schema (400 and 422 both declare a nested `error` object). This is a sixth distinct answer to the running bad-id-behaviour question across this capability family (previously seen: silent 200 half-success, clean 400 with nested error, bare 404 {success:false}, 404 {error:...} with no success key, 502). reorder_folders' 400 is its own seventh variant: flat body, no nested error object, generic message that doesn't name the bad id.

GROUP_ID STRING VS INTEGER: not returned by reorder_folders itself (its success body carries no folder data at all), but the read side used to verify it (list_folder_contents) shows the split within a SINGLE response: `folders[].group_id` is the plain integer 2615, `self.contents[].group_id` is the string "3452", for the identical folder ids in the identical call. Confirms the group_id serializer inconsistency is not just cross-capability but can appear twice in one payload from one capability.
